cards.prompt: Your Bank emails from **@yourbank.example**. Label four warning signs in this email.
cards.explanation: The address isn't `@yourbank.example` (**fake sender**), the subject is **rushing you**, it says **"Dear Customer"**, and the button is a **hidden link** to `yourbank-verify.example`.

items.label: "Claim your prize: pay a small fee"

cards.explanation: Asking for codes, prize fees and deadlines are phishing signs. The real address sending you to the app is fine.

cards.prompt: You're expecting a parcel. A text from "Parcels": **"Missed delivery. Pay $2.50 within 1 hour: parcels-fee.example"**

choices.text: Pay it. You really are waiting for a parcel
choices.consequence: The link leads to a fake page that keeps your card details.

choices.text: Reply to ask which parcel it is
choices.consequence: The reply goes to the scammer and shows your number works.

choices.text: Ignore the link and check in the Parcels app
choices.consequence: The app shows your parcel is on its way. No fee.

cards.explanation: A small fee, a deadline and an unfamiliar link are scam-text signs, even when you are expecting a parcel. Check in the official app.

cards.prompt: A caller from "Your Bank's fraud team" asks you to read out the code just texted to you.

choices.text: Read out the code so they can protect your account
choices.consequence: That code lets them sign in as you.

choices.text: Ask them to say your full name first, to prove it
choices.consequence: Scammers can find names online. Knowing yours proves nothing.

choices.text: Hang up and call the number on the bank's website
choices.consequence: The real bank says nobody called you. Scam stopped.

cards.explanation: Never share a sign-in code. Hang up and call back on a number you found yourself.

cards.prompt: A page you opened from a text has a padlock, and it asks for your **card PIN**.

choices.text: Type the PIN in: the padlock shows the page is safe
choices.consequence: A padlock only means encrypted. Your PIN goes safely to whoever runs the page, and that could be a scammer.

choices.text: Check the logo looks right, then type the PIN in
choices.consequence: A logo can be copied in minutes. And a bank never asks for your PIN on a website.

choices.text: Close it: a bank never asks for your PIN on a website
choices.consequence: Right. Padlock or not, a page asking for your PIN is a scam.

cards.explanation: A padlock only means **encrypted**. It doesn't tell you who runs the site, and a bank **never** asks for your card PIN.

cards.prompt: Your Bank is `yourbank.example`. Real, or not?
cards.explanation: Only addresses ending in `yourbank.example` belong to Your Bank.

cards.prompt: A message says you've won, and asks you to pay a fee in gift cards. What is it?

options.text: A scam: real prizes never cost anything to claim
A real prize: the small fee just covers postage
A competition win you've forgotten you entered

cards.explanation: Real prizes never cost money to claim, and gift cards are a favourite scam payment.
